subject: Agriculture
title: Iceland's Lost Topsoil
description: A short lesson to help you apply Iceland's Lost Topsoil.

hook.text: When Vikings arrived in Iceland in 874 CE, forests and grass covered the island. Within centuries, it was barren.

buildup.text: Settlers cleared trees for timber and grazed sheep on fragile volcanic soil.

discovery.text: Without roots holding it, Iceland's lightweight volcanic soil blew away. Half the island's topsoil vanished.

twist.text: Iceland is still losing soil today. Restoration projects replant trees, but recovery takes generations.

climax.text: The story repeated on Easter Island, Greece, and Haiti. Deforestation and overgrazing follow the same script.

punchline.text: Cut the trees, lose the soil, lose everything.

quiz.question: What happened to Iceland's topsoil after Viking settlement?
options: About half blew away after forests were cleared and sheep grazed the land

details.summary: Iceland has lost over 50% of its vegetation and soils since Viking settlement in 874 AD, primarily due to overgrazing by sheep and deforestation. This topic covers how a fragile subarctic ecosystem was rapidly degraded and the massive ongoing restoration efforts to rebuild Iceland's soil.
details.whyItMatters: Iceland's soil loss is one of the most dramatic examples of how quickly vulnerable soils can be destroyed. The country's soil conservation and restoration programs, started in 1907, are among the world's oldest and most ambitious.
takeaways: Iceland lost over 50% of its vegetation cover and 40% of its soil since 874 AD
Sheep overgrazing on fragile volcanic soils was the primary cause of degradation
Iceland's Soil Conservation Service, founded in 1907, is one of the world's oldest

faq.question: How did Viking settlement lead to Iceland's soil loss?
faq.answer: Vikings cleared birch forests for timber and grazing within decades of settlement. Sheep overgrazed the fragile volcanic soil, destroying the thin vegetation holding it in place. Iceland's harsh winds then eroded the exposed soil—in some areas, meters of soil were stripped down to bare rock.

faq.question: What is Iceland doing to restore its degraded soils?
faq.answer: Iceland's Soil Conservation Service plants erosion-resistant grasses and lupins to stabilize bare surfaces. Birch reforestation projects recreate native woodland. Sheep grazing has been drastically reduced in degraded areas. Progress is slow—restoring soil in subarctic conditions takes generations.
